newsitem.title: CANADA: Aluminum can puts brakes on magnesium growth - CRU.
newsitem.headline: Aluminum can puts brakes on magnesium growth - CRU.

text.p: Although prices will creep back from recent sharp setbacks, overall magnesium consumption over the next few years will be dampened by slow growth in the aluminum beverage can market, analyst Mark Croft of CRU International told the World Magnesium Conference.
"The slow growth in aluminum industry will put the brakes on magnesium consumption growth," Croft said.
Magnesium is used to add properties to aluminum alloy and aluminum sheet used in making beverage cans.
CRU said magnesium demand fell last year by two percent because of a sharp fall in aluminum alloy consumption as consumers destocked.

The use of magnesium in aluminum fell 12 percent, or 20,000 tonnes in 1996. Aluminum accounts for just over half of magnesium consumption, and offtake of magnesium for aluminum applications is only set to grow four percent in the period 1996 to 2000, compared with double digit growth of 10 to 15 percent between now and 2000 for magnesium in diecasting, Croft said.
"Magnesium consumption by the aluminium industry should recover considerably in 1997, and should retain the improved level into 1998," Croft said.

However, Croft did not expect the aluminum restocking cycle to persist into the second half of 1997, and prospects for aluminum canstock remain less than encouraging for the next few years because of tougher competition from plastic bottles.

Consumption of magnesium in steel desulphurization will grow at only a modest pace in the major developed countries, and the key issue will be the uptake of magnesium for desulphurization in CIS, Eastern Europe, Latin America and Australasia.
Overall, CRU expected magnesium consumption to rise six percent this year and four percent in 1998.
The ramp up of Dead Sea Magnesium's new plant will restrain the industry's capacity utilization rates over the next two to three years, Croft said.
The question of Russian stockpile sales of a reported 14,000 tonnes still hangs over the market.

"Under the assumption that this material finds its way out relatively gradually, we still believe that net exports from the CIS and China to the West will decline this year from 1996 levels," Croft said.
